(Black Polarized) - The price is certainly unbeatable when you have to pay $160 for legitimate Oakley Polarized Lenses but two obvious differences exist in theses cheaper replacements. (1) The Lens thickness is approximately 1/2 the thickness of the Oakleys.  This in itself makes the Lenses malleable to fitting within the frame with little effort, but it also feels cheaply made. (2) There is obvious field distortion that does not exist with the original Oakley lenses.  I was able to tell my vision was distorted as soon as they covered my eyes.  To validate the distortion I kept my eyes fixed on a square object and slowly moved my head away and back again and the square shape would lose its crisp edges in favor of round edges and then back again.  Overall these replacements will work for me but I don't trust what I see and do not plan on driving or playing an fast action sports with these on.

I own five pairs of Keen shoes so it's fair to say I'm a fan of the brand. Four of my pairs are Targhee IIs, which is probably the most well-known Keen, so comparing the Koven to the Targhee II would probably help most of the folks familiar with the brand. But first, be forewarned about the Koven: It does NOT fit like your standard Keen.

Size: The Koven is at least a half size smaller than the same size in the Targhee II. I normally wear size 10.5, but in Keen is need a size 11. I own the Targhee II in mid and low, in 11D and 11E (standard width and wide), and with the Koven I needed an 11.5E. Still, the Koven in 11.5E fits slightly more narrow than the Targhee II in 11D.

The Koven is a slightly lighter weight hiker than the Targhee II. It is NOT waterproof (no "Keen Dry") so it definitely breathes better. I actually bought this instead of the Merrell Moab Ventilator as I wanted a low-cut ventilated shoe to use at work. That's not to say, however, that the WP versions are particularly hot--I use the Targhee II here in Honolulu, where it was 91 degrees today with a RH of 80%, and my Targhee II Mid hikers felt fine. The Koven's breathability, however, is appreciated.

The Koven, while still cushioned, has a much thinner/lighter feeling sole than the Targhee II, which definitely has more "substance" to it when your heel strikes the ground. The Targhee just feels tougher. I haven't worn the Koven for a full shift yet but I can tell now that while decent, it won't be as comfortable or confidence-inspiring as my Targhee.

Also, and this is just my opinion, but the Koven isn't as attractive in person as it is in online pictures. I definitely prefer the look of my Targhees.

Overall, there's nothing bad about this shoe; my problem is that, unlike my other Keens, there's also nothing spectacular about it. If I had paid full price for it I'd probably return it, but I got it during the awesome 30% off Amazon sale, and that was 30% off the already discounted Amazon price. I paid $60 for this, so I cannot complain. I'll probably just wear them out at work and I don't see myself ordering another pair.

The only reason I ordered these instead of the Merrell Moab Ventilator, particularly considering the semi-critical reviews of the Koven here on Amazon, was the price. The Merrell is $10 more on Amazon than at Sports Authority ($89.99 locally) but SA doesn't have the wide version; Amazon had the Koven for $60 with discounts. Truth be told, the Merrell and it's Vibram sole is probably superior the Koven, so I'll probably just end up ordering it and alternating pairs throughout the week--that, or using the Koven for chores where I don't want to scuff/dirty my Targhees or Moab.

I really expected to love these shoes, based on the reviews, and based on my satisfaction with my Keen H2 sandals. Alas, the leather part is way too roomy for my foot. I wear a solid 8.5 Med., leaning a little towards the wide side, but not wide enough for wide width shoes. I LOVE the footbed of these sandals -- it is a perfect fit for my foot, and very comfortable. A few reviews have complained that it's too hard, but I didn't find it to be so; it is leather over cork, and the cork has some give, so there is enough cushioning. Mind you, they're not super cushy like some Tevas or other sandals can be. The feel is similar to a Birkenstock, in my opinion.

The problem for me is the leather straps that go over the top of the foot are way too roomy, and so when walking it feels like my foot is in danger of sliding off the foot bed. They don't hold the foot in securely. You can adjust the ankle strap, and that helps, but the upper part of the foot still slides around. Unfortunately, I was so in love with the foot beds that when I got the shoes and just walked around the house, I talked myself into believing they were OK. As soon as I walked outside for any distance, I realized they were a problem, and now it's too late to return them. Sigh. I googled "how to shrink leather," and I may try some of those remedies (basically, wetting the leather and letting it dry) but since they're supposed to be waterproof, I don't know if that will help. I doubt that an 8 would work for me, given the footbed is a great fit, but it might have worked better. On the basis of my experience, I would recommend sizing down or ordering two sizes to compare, unless you have a particularly wide or high foot.

Oboz is not normally a go to brand for me, but I do like these Traverse Low's. I normally wear an 11 or 11.5 in most shoes, and in the slightly more narrow Oboz Yellowstone II I definitely wear an 11.5... so that is what I went for on the Traverse. I am sensitive to the lift in many of these types of shoes as I spend much time in shoes which have nearly zero or neutral lift (Vibram FiveFingers). The back to front lift is about 6 mm based on feeling alone--Oboz does not have that particular spec on their site.

It is helpful to also know these things about the Traverse BDry--it will not stretch out very much, so it is best to get the size you may wear right out of the box (based on another comment this is due to the BDry membrane). Additionally, it might take some users time to get used to the hard heel. Oboz seems to have at least two platforms that have this characteristic -- those like the Yellowstone and these both have pretty hard heels (more info on sole configuration is found on their site). Going from the slipper like comfort of my FiveFingers to these more structured shoes is jolting, but only for about 2 minutes--I quickly acclimate to the different feel.

As for weatherability, I have sloshed around in the muddy yard, and through puddles without any moisture creeping in. Then, cleaning is simple--just rinse them off under running water. The outside seems to dry moderately quickly. Some have complained about slippery soles, and initially I did notice that effect, particularly on wet painted floors and plastic decks, but with only slight wear on the soles, grip has improved--and I feel perfectly secure and safe walking around in these. Wearing them for a couple of weeks, nothing is coming apart, so they seem pretty sturdy and built to last.

I will be looking forward to trying these out in some snow in the next couple of months! They would seem to be a good choice for cooler and wetter weather hiking and trekking.

I purchased this and the small Darcey at the same time to replace an old Samsonite carry-on and decided to return this one and keep the Darcey. I was looking for a roomy, lightweight case with exterior pockets (specifically a pocket big enough for documents, magazines, etc). Most of the time my only luggage is my carry-on even on extended international trips so durability was also very important. This bag fulfilled most of my criteria, but ultimately was not the right one for me.

Pros:
-Lightweight
-Durable Kipling nylon
-Can pack a whole lot
-Multiple interior compartments
-Multiple exterior pockets

Cons:
-Duffle straps are an inconvenience when you need to access the main compartment quickly. I understand this is "duffle" bag, but due to the dimensions I would have been wheeling this most of time (if not all the time)
-Exterior pockets are small; good for toiletries and packing a lot of smaller items. My personal preference is to have a large exterior compartment.
-2-wheels; this is also a matter of personal preference but I found the Discover less smooth and less maneuverable than the Darcey spinner
-Seems a tad larger than standard carry-on, especially if it were completely packed.

I did not attempt to actually pack the bag so cannot speak to the stability issues when standing upright, but I can see how that could be an issue with such a lightweight bag that is sitting on 2-wheels.

Sadly, that's where the awesomeness ended. The front pinched my toes and they felt crunched after just a bit of walking around the house. So, instead of spacers we added some thin foam pieces in the front to cushion the toes. Wore them to work today and after barely 100 steps from the car to my desk I have an open blister on the back of the left heel and the start of one on the right! Ok, we'll break out the band-aids we keep in the desk drawer and put some of those on. The ball of the foot is also not cushioned so lets add a round little gel piece for that one part on the inside of your foot that bears the majority of your weight. Now, I spend the majority of my day at my desk with the occasional trip to the printer or restroom and a trip down to the cafeteria for some coffee, yet barely half way through the day the front of the left shoe is completely separated - what the heck?! Inspect the right shoe and find that it's also starting to separate along the outer side! Clearly this is a lovely case of getting what you paid for. At $15 I wasn't expecting anything fantastic but I at least thought they'd make it one day. Instead, 2 foam inserts, 2 gel inserts, 4 band-aids, and 2 pieces of day saving double stick tape on the right shoe later - the dumpster has a new pair of shoes.

These are good for what they are: a cheap knock-off of Maui Jim sunglasses. From the front this model is a dead ringer for one of the Maui Jim models (which I also own), though the temples are a bit different and this lacks an inner frame across the top of the lenses that the Maui Jim's have. As cheap sunglasses, though, these do a very reasonable job.

But there's a reason why even the cheapest reading glasses are made of glass, not cheap plastic. The reading part works well enough, though the view is not so clear that I would want to read with these for an extended period of time. The border between that part of the lens and the rest of it, however, is visible to the wearer as a slightly blurry line. It isn't directly in the field of vision but can be quite annoying. (The same border on the Maui Jim's is invisible to the wearer.)

I can recommend these if you need a cheap pair of sunglasses for occasional use and very occasional, quick reading. But for regular sunglasses or extended reading you should pay for glass lenses.

Note: these are not a newer version of the Biom Walk, which has been discontinued. They look a bit like them, but as I discovered, they are Nothing like that amazingly comfortable show.

I started noticing that my wonderful Biom Walk 1.1 shoes were starting to show wear, not to the point where I would throw them out, but definitely not looking as spiffy as before. This is after all, after 3 years or so and I wear them every day. The older Biom Walk fit like a glove; for once my narrow feet felt like they had found their perfect match. So, I started thinking I should really get another pair before they disappear or you know, make them "better" and ruin an already perfect thing. But, I never did pick up a second pair, that is until now.

This Biom Grip shoe is not made from yak leather, so they're not as soft and form fitting right out of the box. They are also somewhat wider than my old walking shoes and sadly, in my opinion at least, not as cool looking. But worst of all, whereas the older ones felt great right out of the box, (i.e. no break in period needed,) these feel stiff and ill fitting. Strangely, the inserts feel as if the "support" is in all the wrong places: instead of arch support it feels as if there's a random bump in the middle of the shoe right next to the ball. I'm not sure what they were going for here. Now these might conceivably break in, but I don't want to wear them out of the house as then I will own them. So, (as Yoda might say,) return them I will. Note: I was trying to find something that most resembled my walkers. I now believe Ecco has completely discontinued making the shoes I had and these are really a different line.

And lesson learned: you can buy just about anything on the Internet, but shoes, not so much. And as for Eccos, the jury is out, but these replacements seem run of the mill, while my old Biom Walk 1.1's were really something special.

I always wanted a Barbour waxed cotton jacket & saved up for it. Next time I am saving up to have the jacket waxed by the company!  Not worth the mess! This was a great purchase, especially with the 20% coupon bringing the price down under $100. I was about to use my REI 20% coupon for these boots on REI.com, but at the last minute I thought to check Amazon, and I'm glad I did. Saved about $25.
The boots are very comfortable, especially once broken in after a couple solid hikes. I require a wide size, and when I got these they seemed a bit to snug at first. However, as I predicted after I wore them around the house for several hours I could tell they'd likely loosen up a bit on the trail. And when I hiked in them I wasn't disappointed. I've given these boots a real beating on some tough trails with big elevation gain and loss, as well as over granite rock fields. The stayed pretty dry even in moderate rain and snow, but eventually your feet will get wet if you're in serious wet conditions for long (true for most true hiking boots vs mountaineering boots).

I've been on a long search for the right shoes and heard Mizunos were good. I tried these because they seemed to provide a good balance of minimal shoe with a bit extra padding. I have a size 9 foot, extra wide, so ordered these in a size 10. There is about half a thumb's-width of room between my toe and the end of the shoe. When laced up loosely, these shoes are fine width-wise, however the ankle slips to the point where it seems dangerous to run in them. If I tighten the ankle then the width is too narrow. The laces seem very unforgiving.

However I'd say the part that really rubbed me the wrong way about these shoes (literally) is a plastic sort of piece at the end of the tongue of the shoe near the toes. It rubs right along the bone behind my big toe on both feet, and after running only eight miles in them developed a blister that popped and bled through the shoe. I didn't realize how bad it was until looking down mid-run and seeing a bright red splotch of blood on my bright white shoe. The tongues also do not have a loop at the top, only at the mid-section, so you cannot lace them properly to keep the tongue from moving around, so even when trying to adjust the tongue of these shoes multiple times to keep the plastic bit from rubbing, the tongue would eventually move on its own anyway, causing one of the most horrific blisters I've ever had.

As far as arch support, it's minimal, which is good for my flat, wide feet, but you'll need to be aware of this if you have high arches. The padding is definitely comfortable. I had blisters on the bottom of my feet from other shoes, but with these I could run and the old blisters didn't hurt at all in the Mizunos because of the padding, so that was nice. It's just a shame that the tongues in these shoes are so incredibly uncomfortable.

I've been buying and wearing Oakley SI boots since the '90's with generally positive experiences with design, workmanship, etc. However, this new boot is a stark turn in the wrong direction.
1) Boot seems designed for aesthetics now at the expense of basic field use characteristics. Case in point - Previous iterations of this boot had connecting fabric along the sides of the tongue which prevented dirt, pebbles, etc from entering the boot. New model has a minimal strip and now everything easily gets inside the boot. The new philosophy seems to be "who cares how it works/feels as long as it looks good."
2) Parts of the tread are weakly attached to the sole of the boot, a few hours of normal walking around and you are looking for the Gorilla Glue to re-attach a loose piece of waffle-shaped rubber to the bottom of your boot.
3) New upper material is thin and stiff, so although the boot is light, it isn't comfortable and doesn't feel rugged. The boot feels like you are wearing the cardboard box the boots came in and not the boot itself.
The success of this line of boot has spawned numerous competitors and Oakley might be a victim of their own success. Although they helped popularize this particular style of footwear, their decision to emphasize looks over usefulness has cost them at least one longtime customer.

So I thought I'd check out the Mojitos because I like everything about the Zen except the styling for casual settings IS on the technical side.  Unfortunately the Mojito is scaled back in all the other important supportive and comfort features that the Zen has.  For instance there is no polymer cushion for the ball of the foot.  The heal seems to be identical but that's where the cushion stops.  All you get under your toes is rubber, and because of that your ball is now at least a half inch lower in relation to the heal as it compares to the Zen, which feels weired. This $144 shoe is totally crushable offering no support whatever.  Aestheticly it great, if you want a casual Zen, but why does "casual" have to mean flimsy like a slipper, especially from a company who sells to people who probably apriciate the value of flexible but supportive shoes ? The shoes did stink after 3 - 4 weeks of running in the mud and treading small streams, but hey, a cold delicate cycle in the washing machine and you're good to go. I also experienced a small blister on my left achilles heal; not too bad as my skin toughened within the week, and I was able to wear them fine with no more hotspots thereafter. They serve me well! Only complaint is that on a couple points on the outsole of both shoes, the lugs have separated from the midsole slightly, hence the 4 stars, but nothing a little shoe goo couldn't handle! I just hope that in later versions they tackle that outsole issue.

Of course it's beyond the return period so I guess I get to repair it myself and live and learn: sometimes you DON'T get what you pay for. What can you learn from my experience? Go ahead and buy this purse...it really is a great bag for travel and everyday use, BUT when you receive it, give the fabric a good once over and check for weakness in the stitching. I have been using this bag for 5 months. I agree with those here who say the bag smells when first removed from the packaging, but it does go away. The pockets are convenient, the material does not look hideously cheap. Most importantly, my 12oz OXO personal coffee thermos and my Polar Bottles fit in the outer pockets! (This is important if you commute by subway.)
The first thing I did was remove all three straps. Then I attached one of the two non-adjustable straps to where the adjustable strap had been, but hooking the lobster clasps from the strap onto the lobster clasps from the bag. This made the bag into a shoulder bag that hangs in just the right place, without having a bunch of straps I didn't want!
So, here's my main complaint about this bag: The hardware. The lobster clasps keep breaking. The ones attached to the bag both broke. Each time this happened, I was walking around my purse literally went crashing to the ground. (Also, I can't seem to remove the halves that remain attached. So I have 2 broken clasps on the bag right now.) As a work-around, I am attaching the clasps from the handle onto another metal part. Also, one of the grommets from the handle popped off right away, so I am using the other handle (luckily there are two). I think one of the lobster clasps on that one broke too. I realize that I'm using the bag in a "custom" way, and that as occasional subway commuter I may put more wear-and-tear on it than others may, and I also realize this is not a very expensive purse, but nonetheless all this broken hardware is not meeting my expectations.

I will consider myself lucky if the bag makes it another month. Until then I'll be walking around with it, and its unstylish broken clasps (pictured here).

I'm so sad! Over the years I've loved Keds. First I loved them from afar and would buy the wannabe off-brands from Payless and Target when the real thing was too expensive. I love the style with everything, they come in my hard-to-find wide size, and, most importantly, they lasted.

But this time, like others have reported, the rubber outer around the sole started pulling away within a month tops. I probably do more walking than most people, but when I got my previous pair of Champions a couple years ago, this wasn't a problem, and I was walking and wearing them more than I am now. Back then, the sole wore down smooth and just thinned out over time. This pair, though, the sides are pulling away from the insole, the whole bottom sole is popping out from the bottom, and I could flip the rubber outer up and put my finger between the two. They're actually falling apart. They're exploding unwearably. There's no point to spending this much money on the real thing anymore when the off-brands last at least as long.

Dear Dr. Martens,

I felt compelled to write your company and tell you how extremely disappointed I am with the quality of your boots. I am 39 years old and when I was a kid your company was highly respected for making quality boots that lasted forever. Sadly your company has turned into a mockery of your once respected name.

As an adult I am required to wear steel-toe shoes due to insurance reasons where I work. However, I do not do any form of hard labor. I am an avionics technician. Several years ago, when my company mandated that the workers start wearing steel-toe shoes, we all sighed. However, my first thought was Dr. Martens. I immediately bought a pair of Dr. Martens 1919 which was perfect because although they were not truly safety rated boots they would pass our inspection for steel toe shoes and were not as bulky.

I wore those boots for about 3 and half years. I would have continued to wear them if it was not for the two holes that wore into each side of the one boot. Although I expected them to last longer I was not that upset since I almost got 4 years out of them. During my time of wearing them many of my co-workers thought the boots looked great and were impressed that they lasted so long and several of them bought Dr. Martens based on my experience. Mind you, there are 3000 employees that work at my company and we all hate steel-toe shoes and hate that we are being forced to wear them. Especially since the work we do does not risk our feet. So we are all always looking for better quality or lighter shoes.

After my experience, I decided to buy a pair of 8761's, they looked like they would last much longer and they cost even more money $140.00. I was excited to get them and as I did with my first pair I would regularly tell people at work that they would get more out of their money with Dr. Martens boots then they would get from other brands. Well all of my talk came to an end rather quickly with the 8761's. Within 6 months the damn soles started coming apart. People at work that were wearing generic Wal-Mart shoes were getting longer lasting foot wear then my expensive Dr. Martens. I felt like a fool and felt like I had been robbed. The company I work for gives their employees $65.00 a year toward shoes. I had wasted 2 years worth of money on a pair of boots that did not even last 6 months. You should see the boots now they look like they are 15 years old yet they are maybe a year and a half old.

Anyway, it is time for me to buy another pair of shoes. A lot of the guys at work have been having some good luck with steel toe shoes from Keen. I think I will give them a try. I don't feel like throwing my money down the toilet. I will leave that for un-informed pop punk teenagers that want to look cool, not the working class.

I am not a trail runner, I am an Ultralite Backpacker. About a year ago I was looking for a new hiking boot.and, unable to find anything I really liked, stumbled onto the Loan Peak 2.0 (the previous version of this 2.5 update). I was so impressed with v2.0 as a backpacking shoe that I wrote an extensive view and left it on the Altra website, and wrote something similar for Amazon. In effect, they are the hands down best hiking shoe for maintained trails like the PCT I've ever come across...at least for me. So, I was out on the PCT this season and it seemed like every through hiker I ran across was wearing them. One of them told me they were the "Goto" shoe for the PCT now! So I of course figured that was all because of my reviews...because why not?  Anyway, I just bought this new version 2.5 and have a hike coming up on the JMT in a week, so I'll report back after that if there are any problems, but at first blush these seem like a nice improvement over the 2.0. The toe box has been reduced a little, but hopefully not enough to ruin them. The rest of the show has been snugged up a little around the mid foot, which is a good idea. When I slipped my foot into the shoe, it felt perfect...very much like my well-broken in v2.0.  As was the case with the v2.0, I use the gater catcher on the heel all the time, hiking through sandy trails. There is a kind of lip on the back of the sole that tends to throw sand up onto your calf. Not sure why it is there, but the gaters keep the sand from going into the shoe. The shoes are very light weight, much better than clunky old hiking boots. They dry out very quickly. I soaked my v2.0s a couple of times on the trail, and they were dry in no time. The v2.0 was exceptionally comfortable... like hiking in bedroom slippers. It's the only shoe I didn't feel like taking off at the end of a long hike. The soles are very solid on rock. Theyy grab onto granite as well as my soft-rubber rock climbing shoes. The rock guard in the sole works really well. You can step on pebbles and small rocks and barely feel a thing. The shoes have internal straps near the mid-foot for stability so that you don't slide foward going down hill. I never rammed by toes into the end of the toe-box going downhill. Lateral stability is OK for me. Runners might need more than hikers.  As far as wear and tear -- I probably have four or five hundred backpacking miles on my v2.0s and they aren't dead yet. I keep waiting for them to crap out on me, but they just hang in there.  One downside is the Company itself, which is not good. Their customer support is absolutely horrible. If you end up with a bad pair of shoes, you better hope you ordered them from Amazon because the Altra sure isn't going to help you.  Later - as promised, I am reporting on the JMT trip I used the 2.5 shoes on. Honestly, they are very close to the v2.0. And they are built a little better. however, after 40 miles of hiking, I got s blister. I never came close to a blister in the v2.0, not in hundreds of miles. I recommend flexing your foot forward in these if you buy them to see if there are any creases that press down over the ball of your foot, and how much pressure is there, and take note of that.  Finally, on Thelma side, the v2.5 has a stiffer rock guard, which is a nice addition, but the fabric for the she has been changed to something that appears to be more rugged but is also more porous when it comes to sand. At the end of my day, despite gaters, I was pouring out a good quarter of a cup of sand from each shoe. So there are pluses and minuses to this upgrade.

I ordered a half size large, because I know soccer shoes tend to be too thin, but it was still way too tight for the toes.  I went ahead and measured length and width with a ruler, and looked figures up online.  The width (for 11.5) was 3.855" when 4.2" is appropriate.  That is about 8% too skinny.  The effect was like cramming my toes into vacuum-wrap, and the toes still couldn't quite reach the end (they shouldn't, since I ordered a half size up).  I did not need to walk around in them; they were clearly not fitting.  Note: If you are used to skinny soccer shoes (they are the norm), you can play fine in them 1.5 – 2 sizes large.  The exaggerated V-shaped toe applies enough pressure to other parts of your foot (smaller toes, top, and sides of feet) that your foot will not slide around in a properly tied shoe.  There is the added benefit that you can safely "toe" the ball, because there is half an inch between your toes and the toe of the shoe.  It can hurt your foot and make the shoe degrade quickly if you play much soccer, so I am looking for an alternative instead of reordering larger.  UPDATE: I eventually ordered a 12.5 in these shoes, which will fit okay with new insoles.  They are long but wearable, and they should last a while (last Adidas pair were good for 6 years of mid-level use for me).  It's hard to find soccer shoes with a normal length to width ratio, unless you jump into the $100+ range.  The good news is they stretch a little, so I almost could have fit in a 12.  Maybe.  Having played with them, I noticed that the sole is rather weak.  This is fine on firm ground fields, but it's a pain with the artificial turf I've had to play on lately.  One blister is trying to form on my right pinky toe, which is situated halfway over the edge of theinsole and gets extra friction from that.  Overall, a decent option for forty bucks (given that most alternatives have the same issue), but not something to jump at.  For one alternative, at my in-store quests, I noted Bravia cleats seemed to fit with a more normal width, but they seemd less durable and weren't available in the right size, and I decided to go with these above.

I've been a fan of FitFlops since they debuted, and have enjoyed wearing both the sandals and the boots for casual, run-around comfort. My "good" shoes are usually Italian or French heels and sandals of high-quality build, but if you're going to run around in casual clothes, in a place bound by concrete, like New York, FitFlop comprises a great option.

In recent years, I've returned several pair, because it seems FitFlop is now building for the wide-foot market, no matter what model one chooses. I consider myself a solid medium width with a long last; as such, cheaper closed shoes don't usually work for me. I am also a 10-10.5/41 in closed shoes, and have consistently bought size 9 in FitFlops, because the length is equally generous, and I found myself tripping in a 10--save for boots, which leave consideration for sock wearing.

I am also done with wearing the thong-type FitFlops. They may feel good at first, but eventually, they irritate the space between the first and second toes. I tried to have my expert shoe-repair guy tighten them a little when they've stretched, but particularly with the suede models, that's not a sustainable solution. Once that bit of the thong stretches, there's no brisk walking on these; and brisk walking should be what FitFlops do best!

So another summer, and another attempt to find a FitFlop that doesn't fall off or irritate my foot. In past summers, I tried the Banda, Lulu and DeLoop models. The front-foot band was too narrow in depth, and didn't seem to keep the front of my foot solidly into the sandal. I'd tried on a couple of the horizontal models in the wrong color at a local discounter. The Loosh was hard and irritating in the wrong places, and the Biker Chic seemed to work, so I purchased these on Amazon, feeling they were a possible solution.

Out of the box, the size 9 was comfortable, if a bit snug in the forefoot. I walked around at home with them, and used my shoe stretcherto break the front in a bit more, and now they're perfect! Only one issue: one of the small, square studs fell off the shoe within the first day. They have prongs, and I'll try to re-mount it somehow. As it was one of the smaller studs, I'll try not to get too worked up if it won't re-mount. I think the more blinged-out FitFlops are a little too middle-aged-Florida for my taste, so the black-on-black studs on the Biker Chic model are just enough embellishment, without shouting "mall walker." With a foot my size, who wants undue attention called to one's foot?

The newest Aztek Chada and Amsterdam look like good next-pair options for me, but to be honest, I'm not sure a shoe that is mostly plastic/rubber is worth $130-140. I will probably try them when they are more reasonably-priced. Like others, I think FitFlop should find a way to line their sandal soles in leather; I'd probably think about the "mostly plastic" less. They should also take back old Fitflops for recycling; I hate the idea of throwing out a fully-intact sole for stretching or failure of the leather bands.

Lots of slots for lots of cards.  One nice aspect is that, with slots on both sides, this is a good card case for left-handed people.  Maybe you other lefties out there carry your wallets differently than me, but my last small wallet had card slots on only one side, and I would slide it into my right back pocket with the cards towards me and the slot openings up.  When I would pull it out of the pocket, the thing would be upside down.  If I put it in my pocket with the cards away from me and the outer slots up, it would come out of the pocket right side up but with the cards on the side away from me.  With this case, it will come out of either back pocket right-side up with your most-used cards on the side that faces you.  But if you are going to use it as a wallet, be aware that you are going to get *maybe* seven bills folded in half in the middle slot, and you might have to take the cards out to let the case be flexible enough to get the bills in.

I bought these sandals specifically for hiking in the backcountry of the Colorado Rockies. It was between the Toachi 2 and the Terra FI 4, I ended up choosing the Toachi for two reasons, the water draining feature which is really awesome since I have to forge through creeks and lakes often when off trail and the plastic clip which is great for everyday use. When I got this sandal out in the backcountry I found out this sandal is totally designed for boat use. It has absolutely no use in the backcountry since there is very little tread and the foot bed is very flimsy. I've taken this sandal out in the backcountry four times on 10-15 mile hikes often with no trail and every time I have taken a fall because of the sandals and I almost never fall. The last fall I took I did some damage to my toes and I will be out for recovery for at least six weeks before I can aggressively start hiking again. For everyday use this sandal is very comfortable but that's not what I need. I found a pair of Obern's on Ebay but they are a half size to big so if they do not work I'll give the FI 4 a try and see how they compare to the Obern which was a bomb proof sandal.

Well...

Okay, so let's start with the look. They're super cute, but sophisticated and the heel adds that extra touch of scholarly class. The feel of the material is very nice (I'm avoiding anything too suede or too shiny), and it's been good around water and such. They do scuff pretty easily, which I wouldn't have mind as much of these had been my throwaway shoes that I got for $10.

As for the fit, I was a bit let down. My feet are shaped funny so they're narrow in some places and wide in others. I can usually get away with a regular fit with some lace readjustments and a clever use of insoles. This boot fit everywhere just fine (I wear a 6 and ordered a 6 after a 6.5 was way too big) except for a slightly too snug fit at the sides of my big and little toes. After just a few hours of walking, my feet were already hurting and there were blisters when I got home; and this is coming from the girl who can comfortably run in 4in heels all day. My hope is that with a little bit more time and use to break these in, they will become my new favorite pair of shoes.

All in all, it's a cute pair of lace up leather booties. They're not as comfortable as I hoped they'd be for the money I threw in for them, but I'm hoping they can be broken in further and it's just a case of "gets better the longer you use it". I bought these with a gift card so I technically didn't spend much on them, but having wanted these before having acquired the card, I must say I'm a little dissatisfied.

I guess I am too naive about women's shoes. After spending hours in a shoe warehouse looking for ANY cross-trainers in wide widths and leaving with no options, I did some research online, then came to Amazon where I spent even more hours reading reviews. I purchased four pairs of cross-trainers and not a single one worked. Learn from my mistakes.

As a reference, my bigger foot (left) is 9.5" from big toe to heel, the ball is the widest part of my foot at just over 4" and my heel is 2.5" wide. I typically wear a size 7.5. I have a bunion on my left foot, very high arches, and my pinkie toes are a bit hammertoed from years in ill fitting high heels. I am making a concerted effort to wear better shoes, even if it costs me more. Unfortunately shoemakers refuse to recognize women with foot widths over 3". I ordered all these shoes in 7.5 D because I didn't see them any wider. That may have changed by the time you are reading this. Zappos tells me I should have ordered a size 8. Take my review for what it is: my one-time opinion.

Pair 1: NB 797 7.5 D. As I took these out of the box I knew they were doomed. Seriously, these don't look like "wide" shoes at all, I wish I'd gotten the "normal" B width to compare. This must be a joke, right? After putting them on I noticed what is a constant problem for me. The toe box of the shoe is too narrow, while the heel/opening is gargantuan. Pinkie toes are pinched and bunion is sensitive. Length is also cutting it close, like half a thumb left up front. Seems low on the sides but that's probably for the lateral movement. Also, the insole seems to be floating in the shoe. It's not too narrow, it's just not glued down so it seems like it might keep coming out every time I take the shoe on and off.

Pair 2: NB 711 7.5 D. These are the cutest in my opinion. I seriously want these to work. But they look so narrow. What. the. heck. Ah, super lightweight, not a lot of seams, narrower heel for sure. Also less padded around the shoe opening than #1. After leaving it on for just a few minutes, my bunion is throbbing slightly. That does not bode well. Length is cutting it close. If this came in an 8 4E, it would be a keeper.

Pair 3: NB 20 Minimus 7.5 D. These are definitely the least appealing to me. I mean they aren't bright white, but not my cup of tea. Anyway. Definitely the widest of the bunch. Ample room on the outside of the foot, it's weird, they sort of lean in, in a way that makes my bunion feel the bottom seam of the shoe. So it's not the pressure from the top or side that is irritating it, it's the lip of the shoe insert. Oh, there's no insert. Well I guess just where the upper and lower parts of the shoe meet. Looking at it you would be able to tell what I'm talking about; it definitely leans. The sides and back come up a little higher on the ankle, still not above the outer fibula bone-end, or the interior navicular bone-bump, so I like it more. I'm also clearly a dum-dum for ordering a 7.5. Still, this feels the best so far except for lean and it's effect on my bunion. Is the lean important to "minimal" shoes? Also, the box mentions running, which is not what I'm interested in. The listing online says cross-trainer.

Pair 4: Asics Gel Unifire 7.5 D. These are also a joke. The leather detail work on the uppers irritate my bunion from the start. The toe box is too narrow for the rest of my digits too. Actually the length on this seems better, but that is the only thing that is okay with this shoe. It feels nicely padded, I'll give it that. A big nope, all in all.

So all four of these go back, what a delight. This isn't a waste of my money and time at all, nooooo. I have now ordered NB Mens 623s and 608 in both 2E and 4E. I've also ordered from Zappos the Asics Gel 180 in 2E for women and the Asics Gel Acclaim in 2E for men. I think the biggest problem is Amazon's lack of selection (not even color-wise, just pure options!) at wide widths, and potentially no standardization of sizes, just like clothes. Are wide shoes just the unicorn of footwear or does Amazon just not care?
